The problem with rape, independently on our view on feminism and the veracity of the accusation, is that it's a crime that is almost always perpetrated in private, meaning you have to build a case with nothing but the words of the two persons involved. And both genuine rape and rape accusations, whether founded or not, have huge negative impacts on the lives of the people involved. This means no matter the advancement of feminism or any social justice movement for anything and anyone, it will always come down to who we trust the most : the alleged raper or the raped. So accusing someone of rape will always be an easy way to destroy someone's life, no matter how easily or not it can be disproved, and how real the rape was (that it happened or not is almost irrelevant).

Now, what can we do to limit the cases of both rapes and false rape accusations? I think the first thing we should do is to define the act of rape, and make it clear it is a terrible thing, even in its softer definition (which yet too many people seem not to consider rape), no matter if the two people involved are male or female or all kinds of in between.

It's a human issue, not a feminism issue. And since it has so much psychological impact, and so many people don't report rape and harassment, we absolutely can't know for sure if male or female are more often victims or not, no matter what your preferred source of statistics say.

Please stop it with the "they're not making them illegal, they're just making them hard to acquire" nonsense. Many places DO ban whole types or classes of firearms or effectively ban access for 99% of aspiring legal gun owners.

What constitutes "hard to acquire" is often in practice "impossible to acquire". Some states in the US and some countries are "may issue", meaning they decide whether or not you show a genuine reason or sufficient need to concealed-carry a firearm. There is no set definition for this; some states like New York deny nearly everyone because they have no interest in allowing concealed-carry. Other places have been taken to court for taking too long to ponder a person's reasoning; again, New York state maintains that it can wait up to A YEAR to grant you a license. Imagine putting all that time, money, and effort into passing your driver's test and getting all the paperwork done, waiting a year for your license, and then a judge decides you don't need a car and denies you your license. The constitutionality of "may issue" in the US (specifically Maryland) has been challenged, won in court, overturned by a higher court, denied appeal in the circuit court, and given to the Supreme Court but was denied a place in the docket. Similarly, anything too exotic (automatic rifles, short-barrel shotguns, etc) requires a long process involving the ATF, a background check, approval from the highest ranking person in your local law enforcement, and a $200 fee. This is per firearm, not a one-time thing. Many times the sheriff will be a dick and deny these transactions for pretty much everyone in town, despite many lawsuits being filed for doing so. Don't expect this to change any time soon even in America.

Some places decide you just can't have some guns. In Australia anything center-fire (read: not a tiny .22 rimfire plinker) and made after 1901 requires a "genuine need". Anything semi-auto basically requires you to be a collector, law enforcement, or a professional target shooter. Want more than 5 rounds in your rifle? Too bad, that's only for the government and target shooters. Want a handgun? Gotta have a job that requires its use and spend 6 months on a range. In the United Kingdom, all concealable pistols (barrel length under 30cm or total length under 60cm!) are banned and long-barreled pistols require a license. Anything semi-auto has to be .22 or smaller. Want a shotgun? 2+1 is the maximum ammo capacity so I hope you like your grandpa's Elmer Fudd hunting shotgun. Carry an airsoft gun while trespassing? It's now trespassing with a firearm. Better hope you painted at least half of it a bright color or you're getting another charge. And don't get me started on what constitutes an "assault weapon" in America. Many accessories - some of them cosmetic - scared law-makers so badly that they're straight-up banned in a lot of states (and banned from production entirely in the US from 1994 to 2004). How dare you put scary things on your rifles like GASP! pistol grips or OH DEAR LORD! barrel shrouds. Not to mention you can still dodge state assault weapon laws if you are determined enough with very minimal change in the actual "deadliness" of the gun.

Before comparing gun restrictions to driver's licenses, try educating yourself first. Thank you.
